summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a focused demo for CartoFlow covering structured output (JSON mode), schema enforcement, and function/tool calling. Customer cares about reliable JSON output for downstream parsers, guardrails to avoid hallucinated fields, and ability to call internal tools (address lookups, pricing engine). Discussed hosted vs Dedicated for throughput/cost and VPC for data controls. Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, POC kickoff and sharing prompt set.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start time: 16:30 PST
Duration: 54 minutes (scheduled)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Product), Lena (CartoFlow CTO), Marcus (CartoFlow ML Eng), Priya (CartoFlow PM)

-- Auto-generated summary present --

[00:00] Maya: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick introductions then we'll jump into a live walkthrough of JSON mode and function calls.
[00:20] Lena: Hi, Lena here, CTO at CartoFlow. Marcus and Priya with me. Looking forward — we've got an internal mapping + pricing flow that needs structured responses.
[00:35] Marcus: Hey all. We're evaluating how to get the model to output strict JSON so our parsers don't crash.
[00:45] Ethan: Awesome. That's exactly what we'll demo — JSON schema enforcement, field-level validation, and then function/tool calling so you can invoke your pricing microservice from the model. Bear with the demo, I might fumble a bit with the example prompts.
[01:05] Priya: Also want to understand fallback behaviors — if the model returns invalid JSON, can Redwood re-try or fall back to a simpler template?
[01:20] Ethan: Yes, we'll cover guardrails. There are a few levers: strict schema validation on the server, optional sanitization/postprocess, and automatic retries with constrained templates.

-- Demo start --
[02:10] Ethan: I'm going to open the Console and show the API playground first. Here's a sample prompt we use for CartoFlow: 'Given an address and user preferences, return JSON with fields: normalized_address, lat_long, delivery_window, price_estimate, and notes.'
[02:40] Ethan: Switching JSON mode on, and attaching a JSON schema. (typing sounds) The schema enforces types and required fields.
[03:05] Ethan: Sending a live request to the hosted endpoint now.
[03:20] Speaker 1: Uh it returned a small mismatch — notes came back as an array of objects, our schema expects a string, so Redwood's validator flagged it.
[03:35] Ethan: Right, that's a common transcribe vs type issue — sometimes the LM voce, the LM output uses different structure. Redwood's Console shows the validation error and the sanitized fallback we configured: when validation fails, we run a secondary prompt that forces serializable fields.
[04:00] Marcus: Can we see the raw tokens? We need to know if the LM is hallucinating fields like 'promo_code' that don't exist.
[04:15] Ethan: Yes — Console token trace and the per-token latency are visible. Also we can enable 'strip unknown fields' so any fields not in the schema are dropped before returning to your app.
[04:40] Jordan: Note: that stripping is important for your downstream ETL, customers. But if you need to capture unexpected keys for analytics, we can optionally log them to a secure bucket.
[04:55] Priya: Are those audit logs available in Private deployments? We need to ensure data residency.
[05:10] Maya: Good question — for VPC or on-prem, audit logs can be stored in your account and integrated with your SIEM. We'll share the security doc with details.

[06:20] Ethan: Next I'm going to wire a mock 'pricing' function. In the sandbox I register a function signature: name: calculate_price, args: { distance_km: number, weight_kg: number, service_level: string }. The model can return a function call instead of straight JSON.
[06:50] Ethan: Run sample: model returned a function_call object {"name": "calculate_price", "arguments": {"distance_km": 12.4, "weight_kg": 2.0, "service_level": "express"}}. Console automatically serializes and can invoke a webhook.
[07:15] Lena: If the model returns arguments slightly off, like weight as string 'two', do you coerce?
[07:27] Ethan: We have type coercion rules and validation. By default we reject and surface an error; you can opt in to coercion and an audit trail.
[07:45] Marcus: Latency concerns — if we invoke an external microservice on every token or call, will that blow up p50/p95?
[08:00] Ethan: Function calls are invoked once per model response, not per token. But network latency matters. For high-throughput we suggest Dedicated capacity in the same VPC or colocated region. That keeps p95 low.
[08:25] Maya: We can show a benchmark later — Ethan has a test harness for that.

[09:00] Ethan: I'm going to simulate a bad output and show guardrails: step 1) schema validation fails, step 2) retry with constrained prompt + higher temperature control to zero, step 3) if still invalid, return structured error object.
[09:30] Speaker 2: The demo shows a 2nd attempt fixed the type and added required fields.
[09:50] Ethan: We also have an optional 'explainability' flag that returns the model's rationale as a separate field so your team can see why it chose a particular bracket or price.
[10:05] Priya: That'd be helpful for QA — we can route 'explainability' output to a human review queue.

[11:20] Lena: What about cost? If we lower temperature and force multiple retries, costs go up. What's the recommended pattern?
[11:40] Maya: Typical pattern: enforce schema + stricter decoding (temperature=0) — that keeps retries low. Then use caching for repeated prefixes, and batch calls server-side where permissable. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions — e.g., quantization, batching thresholds, and cache key rules.
[12:05] Marcus: Does Optimize surface token-level cost attribution? We want to know which prompts leak cost.
[12:18] Jordan: Yes, per-request token breakdown and hot-paths. It can recommend moving a step to a function call instead of the LM to reduce tokens.

[13:00] Ethan: Back to function calling — here's the webhook invocation log showing a successful POST to our mock pricing service, response time 120ms, returned price object, and Redwood merged that into final JSON.
[13:30] Marcus: Can the model call multiple functions in a chain? For example, normalize_address then calculate_price then enrich_from_catalog?
[13:45] Ethan: Yes, Redwood supports multi-function workflows. You can model them as sequential calls or orchestrate with a lightweight orchestration layer. We also support transactional semantics — if a later function fails, you can roll back or return partial results depending on policy.

[14:30] Lena: Security: do function calls expose our internal endpoints to Redwood? We need the webhook traffic to stay within our VPC.
[14:45] Maya: In Private mode, webhook traffic can stay inside your network; for Hosted we use secure egress with mTLS and you can whitelist Redwood IPs. We'll put the network diagrams in the security packet.

[15:30] Priya: A weird edge case — what if the model invents a function name? Does Redwood block unknown function names?
[15:45] Ethan: Yes, function registry is explicit. Unknown names are rejected; you decide if unknown calls should be surfaced to a retry or an error. This prevents hallucinated actions.

[17:00] Marcus: On the topic of structured output, we've seen models insert HTML or markdown into fields. Can Redwood strip or escape?
[17:20] Ethan: We have sanitizer pipeline steps — strip tags, escape characters, and enforce max lengths. Also we log sanitized values to an optional bucket if you want to review transformations.

[18:10] Maya: Quick pivot — here's the API call you'd run from your backend. (reads cURL) "POST /v1/generate" with body including schema param, functions array, and callback webhook.
[18:30] Marcus: Are SDKs available? We prefer a Go SDK for our service.
[18:45] Maya: Yes, Go, Python, and Node SDKs. We'll share code samples.

[20:00] Lena: Let's talk deployment options briefly — we might be sensitive to data in transit for PII addresses.
[20:15] Maya: For PII we recommend either Dedicated with VPC peering or Private on-prem. Both support KMS/HSM key integrations, field-level encryption, and audit logs.
[20:40] Priya: Is there an SSO + RBAC integration for per-route permissions? We want only our payments team to access pricing endpoints.
[20:55] Jordan: Yes, Console supports SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and route-level RBAC. You can lock down specific model routes to roles.

[22:00] Ethan: I'm going to run the 'stress' quick bench. Small sample of 100 requests with different addresses to show p50/p95 and how caching helps.
[22:20] Ethan: Results are populating — p50 110ms, p95 420ms on hosted sandbox for this model. With prefix KV cache turned on p95 drops ~60ms. With Dedicated in-region it's typically under 250ms p95 for similar workloads.
[22:45] Marcus: Nice. Can you share the raw benchmark so our infra team can reproduce?
[22:55] Ethan: Yep, will include test harness and seed dataset in the POC artifacts.

[24:00] Lena: Ok process wise, what does a POC look like?
[24:15] Maya: Typical POC is 4 weeks: week 0 kickoff and data prep, week 1 small integration + benchmark, week 2 iterate on prompts and guardrails, week 3 scale tests and run privacy/security checklist. We'll provide an SE or solutions engineer during the POC.
[24:40] Priya: Budget and purchase path? We may start with Hosted then move to Dedicated.
[24:55] Maya: That's common. Hosted for quick validation, then switch to Dedicated when throughput and SLOs need predictability — we have migration guides. Pricing options will be in the sheet I'll send.

[26:00] Ethan: Quick demo of Console 'rollout' feature: you can route 10% to a new model variant with a fallback to baseline model if outputs don't meet quality thresholds. We can tie rollouts to schema regression checks.
[26:30] Marcus: That would help safe-launch new model weights.

[27:10] Speaker 3: (inaudible) something about the KV cache set up — asked how to populate keys for common addresses.
[27:25] Ethan: You can pre-seed cache via API or let it warm up. For deterministic lookups we recommend pre-seeding using a CSV of top N addresses.

[28:00] Priya: Any known issues with function call chaining and stateful cache? For example, when calculate_price calls a catalog service that returns item IDs, do we store those in KV?
[28:20] Ethan: Yes, you can persist outputs into KV and reference them in subsequent calls; ensure TTLs are set carefully to avoid stale data.

[30:00] Maya: Alright time check — about 25 minutes left. Open Q&A.
[30:15] Marcus: Edge case: PDF parsing pipeline returns addresses in weird formats — can the model normalize and also provide confidence score?
[30:35] Ethan: Yes, include a 'confidence' field in your schema; Redwood will record model confidence if you opt in, otherwise you can compute it posthoc using heuristics.

[32:00] Lena: For legal, we need contract language about data retention and deletion.
[32:15] Maya: We'll attach the privacy addendum and the data retention SLAs. In Private mode you control retention.

[33:10] Priya: Any examples of customers doing similar structured output + function calling?
[33:25] Maya: A marketplace we worked with uses function calls for inventory lookups and structured output for checkout JSON — they moved to Dedicated for 99th percentile needs. We'll anonymize that case study in the docs.

[35:00] Ethan: One last demo: enabling 'schema strict mode' which will never return free text in required fields and will surface an error object instead. Here's an example error payload and how to parse it on your side.
[35:45] Marcus: Good — that helps our error handling pipeline.

[37:00] Lena: Recap for me: you will send pricing, security docs, POC runbook + test harness, and we will provide prompts + dataset. Then schedule POC kickoff.
[37:20] Maya: Correct. Also will share SDK snippets and Dedicated capacity options.

[38:00] Priya: One more operational question — how are regressions monitored? If a new model drops accuracy for an extraction field, can we alert?
[38:20] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Optimize supports eval suites tied to deployments. You can run nightly checks against golden prompts and trigger alerts on regression.

[40:00] Maya: Any blocker from anyone?
[40:10] Marcus: None immediate. We need to align on PII approach and cost.
[40:22] Lena: We'll confirm the team for the POC internally and share the dataset.

[42:00] Maya: Ok, next steps and owners inline with action items. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the POC kickoff.
[42:20] Ethan: I'll prepare the benchmark artifacts.
[42:30] Marcus: We'll send sample addresses and confirm network constraints.

[43:00] Speaker 1: Small audio pop, sorry.
[43:15] Priya: Thanks, this was great.
[43:30] Lena: Thank you, Maya and team.
[44:00] Maya: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

-- End meeting --
notes: Demo covered JSON schema enforcement, function calling (webhook invocations), guardrails (strict mode, sanitizers), Optimize suggestions, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs
Customer will start POC after security check and pricing alignment
